# Behaviour: who delegates, for what, and is it changing? (RQ1) {#sec-rq1}

This section reports RQ1 in the order the pre-registration fixes (@sec-methods): first a descriptive anatomy of how conversations divide between the automation and augmentation patterns, then the four confirmatory hypotheses. AEI data are conversations matched to O\*NET tasks, so every number below describes how those conversations are distributed across tasks, occupations and countries; none describes the people who hold the occupations. RQ1's family-wise α of {{< var design.alpha.rq1_total >}} is split as registered: H2 is tested on its own at {{< var design.alpha.rq1_h2 >}}, and {H1, H3, H4} by Holm at family-wise {{< var design.alpha.rq1_family >}}. @tbl-rq1-confirmatory-table gathers every confirmatory coefficient with its unit, standard error, family p-value, Holm level and decision, and @fig-rq1-coefficients draws the same estimates with their confidence intervals. Each hypothesis is reported below with its decision first, then its estimate, interval and p-value, whatever the decision.

## The anatomy of collaboration

@fig-rq1-composition-major and @tbl-rq1-major (@sec-app-supplementary) show the five collaboration patterns by SOC major group in r6 `claude_ai`. They are computed over published cells only, on AEI's published occupation basis (D9), and carry no test or p-value. Usage is concentrated in Computer and Mathematical occupations, which hold {{< var rq1.anatomy.major.m15.usage_share >}} per cent of published major-group usage, and in that group the automation patterns (directive plus feedback loop) account for {{< var rq1.anatomy.major.m15.automation_pct >}} per cent of classified conversations. The next largest groups lean the other way. Arts, Design, Entertainment, Sports and Media ({{< var rq1.anatomy.major.m27.usage_share >}} per cent of usage) has an augmentation share of {{< var rq1.anatomy.major.m27.augmentation_pct >}} per cent. Educational Instruction and Library ({{< var rq1.anatomy.major.m25.usage_share >}} per cent of usage) has {{< var rq1.anatomy.major.m25.augmentation_pct >}} per cent. The highest automation shares belong to groups with little usage: Protective Service at {{< var rq1.anatomy.major.m33.automation_pct >}} per cent and Installation, Maintenance and Repair at {{< var rq1.anatomy.major.m49.automation_pct >}} per cent, with usage shares of {{< var rq1.anatomy.major.m33.usage_share >}} and {{< var rq1.anatomy.major.m49.usage_share >}} per cent. Legal occupations ({{< var rq1.anatomy.major.m23.augmentation_pct >}} per cent augmentation) and Healthcare Practitioners and Technical occupations ({{< var rq1.anatomy.major.m29.augmentation_pct >}} per cent) sit on the augmentation side. The validation pattern, the outcome of H3, is a small part of every group's conversations (@tbl-rq1-major).

{{< include _generated/figures/rq1-composition-major.md >}}

By wage, usage and employment are distributed very differently (@fig-rq1-composition-wage-decile, @tbl-rq1-wage-decile; @sec-app-supplementary). The top decile of the OEWS median wage holds {{< var rq1.anatomy.wage_decile.d10.usage_share >}} per cent of conversations matched to OEWS occupations against {{< var rq1.anatomy.wage_decile.d10.emp_share >}} per cent of employment. The bottom decile holds {{< var rq1.anatomy.wage_decile.d1.usage_share >}} per cent against {{< var rq1.anatomy.wage_decile.d1.emp_share >}} per cent. The automation share does not move monotonically with the decile: it is {{< var rq1.anatomy.wage_decile.d1.automation_pct >}} per cent in the bottom decile, {{< var rq1.anatomy.wage_decile.d2.automation_pct >}} in the second, {{< var rq1.anatomy.wage_decile.d3.automation_pct >}} in the third and {{< var rq1.anatomy.wage_decile.d10.automation_pct >}} in the top decile. This raw gradient pools all task families. H1 asks the narrower, within-family question, so the two need not agree.

By the education a task requires (@fig-rq1-composition-education, @tbl-rq1-education; @sec-app-supplementary), usage sits mostly in the two lowest bins, which hold {{< var rq1.anatomy.education.lt12.usage_share >}} and {{< var rq1.anatomy.education.12_14.usage_share >}} per cent of usage. The highest bin holds {{< var rq1.anatomy.education.ge18.usage_share >}} per cent. The automation share is {{< var rq1.anatomy.education.lt12.automation_pct >}} per cent in the lowest bin, {{< var rq1.anatomy.education.14_16.automation_pct >}} per cent in the middle bin and {{< var rq1.anatomy.education.16_18.automation_pct >}} per cent in the second-highest bin, so the descriptive education profile has no single direction either. Tasks published without an education value carry {{< var rq1.anatomy.education.zero_published_usage.usage_share >}} per cent of usage: they are the tasks published with zero usage.

Usage is also concentrated across tasks (@fig-rq1-lorenz, @tbl-rq1-concentration; @sec-app-supplementary). In r6 `claude_ai`, the largest {{< var rq1.anatomy.concentration.claude_ai.r6.n_tasks_50pct >}} tasks hold half of the usage over {{< var rq1.anatomy.concentration.claude_ai.r6.n_tasks >}} published matched tasks; in r6 `1p_api` the figure is {{< var rq1.anatomy.concentration.1p_api.r6.n_tasks_50pct >}} tasks over {{< var rq1.anatomy.concentration.1p_api.r6.n_tasks >}}. The as-published Gini coefficients and top-share columns are not comparable across releases. r6 publishes usage to coarser precision and keeps its zero-usage tasks in the count. @tbl-rq1-concentration-harmonised therefore puts every release on r6's rounding and drops zero-usage tasks. Even there the suppression regimes differ by release (PAP §5), so differences between releases are not read as changes in the conversations themselves.

## H1: education, wages and the automation share

H1 is {{< var rq1.h1.decision_text >}} at the pre-registered level: the null that β_e or β_w is zero is not rejected at {{< var rq1.holm.h1 >}}, the Holm level at which H1 was tested (@tbl-rq1-confirmatory-table). Within O\*NET Intermediate Work Activities, β_e is {{< var rq1.h1.beta_e >}} pp of automation per year of education (confidence interval [{{< var rq1.h1.human_education_years_mean.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h1.human_education_years_mean.ci_high >}}], p = {{< var rq1.h1.human_education_years_mean.p >}}). β_w is {{< var rq1.h1.beta_w >}} pp of automation per unit of log wage, that is per unit of the log rather than per log point (interval [{{< var rq1.h1.log_wage.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h1.log_wage.ci_high >}}], p = {{< var rq1.h1.log_wage.p >}}). H1's intersection–union p-value, the larger of the two, is {{< var rq1.h1.p >}}. The sample has {{< var rq1.h1.n_rows >}} rows, {{< var rq1.h1.n_tasks >}} task clusters and {{< var rq1.h1.n_occ >}} occupation clusters. β_e has the predicted sign, but its interval includes zero. β_w is opposite in sign to H1's prediction and is not significant at its Holm level. Under PAP §0.2 and clarification C-21 on mixed signs, it therefore neither supports H1 nor contradicts it, and its nominal p-value is not read as evidence at any registered level. The P13 attenuation factor beside β_w is {{< var rq1.h1.attenuation >}}. It is the between-task share of the within-family wage variation, so the spread of wages across a task's occupations removes little of the identifying variation. Both coefficients compare tasks, weighted by the occupations they are allocated to, and do not compare workers (@sec-methods).

Two pre-registered robustness rows are named beside this decision (@sec-robustness, @sec-app-robustness-tables). R24 r5 re-estimates H1 on release r5 `claude_ai`. It is the one row under which H1's p-value, {{< var rob.r24.r5.p_h1.p >}}, falls below H1's Holm level with both coefficients negative: β_e is {{< var rob.r24.r5.human_education_years_mean.estimate >}} and β_w is {{< var rob.r24.r5.log_wage.estimate >}}. As a robustness row it changes no decision (PAP §8.1). R23 replaces the automation share with the mean AI-autonomy score, the other delegation measure that H1 names, in autonomy scale points per unit of each regressor. PAP §4.1 prints a disagreement statement only if each R23 coefficient is opposite in sign to the primary coefficient and nominally significant (PAP §11, C-77). The education coefficient is opposite in sign, at {{< var rob.r23.human_education_years_mean.estimate >}} (p {{< var rob.r23.human_education_years_mean.p >}}). The log-wage coefficient has the same sign as the primary, at {{< var rob.r23.log_wage.estimate >}} (p = {{< var rob.r23.log_wage.p >}}). The condition therefore does not hold, and the statement is not printed.

The following are a post-result diagnostic (PAP §11 D-3); exploratory; not a decision. @tbl-diag-h1-influence (@sec-app-supplementary) re-estimates H1 with groups of occupations left out. Leaving out SOC major group {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_soc_major_15.dropped >}} (Computer and Mathematical, {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_soc_major_15.dropped_weight_pct >}} per cent of H1's row weight) moves β_e to {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_soc_major_15.beta_e >}} and β_w to {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_soc_major_15.beta_w >}}, with an H1 p-value of {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_soc_major_15.p_h1 >}}. Leaving out the largest occupation, {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_top_1.dropped >}} ({{< var diag.h1.leave_out_top_1.dropped_weight_pct >}} per cent of the weight), moves β_w to {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_top_1.beta_w >}}. Leaving out the three largest ({{< var diag.h1.leave_out_top_3.dropped >}}; {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_top_3.dropped_weight_pct >}} per cent) gives β_e of {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_top_3.beta_e >}}, β_w of {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_top_3.beta_w >}} and an H1 p-value of {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_top_3.p_h1 >}}. β_w thus rests largely on the computing occupations. Among the pre-registered robustness rows, those that move the coefficients most are as follows. R26 with GWA fixed effects gives β_e {{< var rob.r26.gwa.human_education_years_mean.estimate >}} and β_w {{< var rob.r26.gwa.log_wage.estimate >}}; R26 with DWA fixed effects gives {{< var rob.r26.dwa.human_education_years_mean.estimate >}} and {{< var rob.r26.dwa.log_wage.estimate >}}. Under R24 r4 and R24 r5, β_w changes sign, to {{< var rob.r24.r4.log_wage.estimate >}} and {{< var rob.r24.r5.log_wage.estimate >}}. R24 `r6_1p_api` gives {{< var rob.r24.r6_1p_api.human_education_years_mean.estimate >}} and {{< var rob.r24.r6_1p_api.log_wage.estimate >}}. R10's upper bound gives {{< var rob.r10.h1_ub.human_education_years_mean.estimate >}} and {{< var rob.r10.h1_ub.log_wage.estimate >}} (@sec-app-robustness-tables).

## H2: measured within-task automation across releases

H2 is {{< var rq1.h2.decision_text >}} at the pre-registered level: the release-level co-condition fails. β is {{< var rq1.h2.beta >}} pp per year (interval [{{< var rq1.h2.trend.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h2.trend.ci_high >}}], task-clustered p {{< var rq1.h2.p_cluster >}}) on the balanced panel of {{< var rq1.h2.n_tasks >}} tasks and {{< var rq1.h2.n_rows >}} task-release rows over r2–r5. That meets the task-clustered condition and has the predicted sign. The release-level wild cluster bootstrap, over all {{< var rq1.h2.n_wild_draws >}} enumerated weight vectors, gives p = {{< var rq1.h2.p_wild >}}, above {{< var rq1.holm.h2 >}}. The release-label randomisation over {{< var rq1.h2.n_release_orderings >}} orderings gives p = {{< var rq1.h2.p_release_label >}} and is descriptive only. The trend is identified from four release cross-sections. As registered (D22), the co-condition is demanding and may be conservative: only a trend that is large relative to release-to-release variation can meet it (@sec-methods). β is the change in measured within-task automation. It includes any change in AEI's classifier, which no release names, and in platform scope (D2, D22; PAP §5). The estimate is therefore not a change in behaviour alone.

The event-style plot (@fig-rq1-h2-release-effects) shows where the trend comes from. Relative to r2, the release coefficients are {{< var rq1.h2.release_effect.r3.estimate >}} pp for r3 (interval [{{< var rq1.h2.release_effect.r3.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h2.release_effect.r3.ci_high >}}]), {{< var rq1.h2.release_effect.r4.estimate >}} pp for r4 ([{{< var rq1.h2.release_effect.r4.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h2.release_effect.r4.ci_high >}}]) and {{< var rq1.h2.release_effect.r5.estimate >}} pp for r5 ([{{< var rq1.h2.release_effect.r5.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h2.release_effect.r5.ci_high >}}]). The measured rise is one r2-to-r3 step followed by a fall. That step coincides with a change in the base of classified conversations. r2's shares are renormalised without `filtered`, while r3–r5 exclude `not_classified` and `none` (PAP §5). Classifier or platform drift therefore cannot be separated from behaviour. The next results are a post-result diagnostic (PAP §11 D-3); exploratory; not a decision. In @tbl-diag-h2-influence (@sec-app-supplementary), leaving out r2 reverses the sign of β to {{< var diag.h2.leave_out_release_r2.beta >}} pp per year (task-clustered p {{< var diag.h2.leave_out_release_r2.p_cluster >}}, wild p = {{< var diag.h2.leave_out_release_r2.p_wild >}}). Leaving out r3, r4 or r5 instead gives {{< var diag.h2.leave_out_release_r3.beta >}}, {{< var diag.h2.leave_out_release_r4.beta >}} and {{< var diag.h2.leave_out_release_r5.beta >}}. Two pre-registered robustness rows run the other way. R22 `api_r3_r5`, the `1p_api` series over r3–r5, gives {{< var rob.r22.api_r3_r5.estimate >}} pp per year ([{{< var rob.r22.api_r3_r5.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r22.api_r3_r5.ci_hi >}}]). R23's H2 part, the autonomy score over r4–r6, gives {{< var rob.r23.h2.estimate >}} autonomy scale points per year ([{{< var rob.r23.h2.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r23.h2.ci_hi >}}]). The latter is labelled confounded with the r6 suppression-regime change (@sec-app-robustness-tables).

{{< include _generated/figures/rq1-h2-release-effects.md >}}

The balanced panel also has a cost, reported here as descriptive (@tbl-diag-h2-influence; @sec-app-supplementary). The D2 rule keeps only tasks published in all four releases. It removes {{< var diag.h2.balancing_removed.n_tasks >}} tasks that are published in some but not all of them, holding {{< var diag.h2.balancing_removed.usage_share_pct >}} per cent of the unbalanced panel's task weight. R22's unbalanced row, which keeps them, gives {{< var rob.r22.unbalanced.estimate >}} pp per year ([{{< var rob.r22.unbalanced.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r22.unbalanced.ci_hi >}}]; @sec-app-robustness-tables).

## H3: validation in high-error-cost occupations

H3 is {{< var rq1.h3.decision_text >}} at the pre-registered level: the null that γ is zero is not rejected; Holm stopped at H1, and p exceeds even H3's level, {{< var rq1.holm.h3 >}} (@tbl-rq1-confirmatory-table). Within O\*NET Intermediate Work Activities, γ is {{< var rq1.h3.gamma >}} pp of validation share (interval [{{< var rq1.h3.error_cost.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h3.error_cost.ci_high >}}], p = {{< var rq1.h3.error_cost.p >}}). The sample has {{< var rq1.h3.n_rows >}} rows, {{< var rq1.h3.n_tasks >}} task clusters and {{< var rq1.h3.n_occ >}} occupation clusters. The error-cost occupations are the legal, health-practitioner and regulated-finance codes fixed in D15. The point estimate is negative, opposite to H3's predicted direction, and its interval includes zero. Under PAP §0.2 it therefore neither supports nor contradicts the hypothesis. The P13 attenuation factor is {{< var rq1.h3.attenuation >}}, the between-task share of the error-cost indicator's within-family variation. The pre-registered rows that vary H3 are reported in full in @sec-robustness, and no generated file ranks them. R27, with the continuous consequence-of-error measure, gives {{< var rob.r27.h3.estimate >}} ([{{< var rob.r27.h3.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r27.h3.ci_hi >}}]). R31, with H1's covariates added, gives {{< var rob.r31.error_cost.estimate >}} ([{{< var rob.r31.error_cost.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r31.error_cost.ci_hi >}}]). R38, with occupation-clustered errors, gives {{< var rob.r38.h3.estimate >}} (p = {{< var rob.r38.h3.p >}}). R10's upper bound gives {{< var rob.r10.h3_ub.estimate >}} ([{{< var rob.r10.h3_ub.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r10.h3_ub.ci_hi >}}]).

## H4: geography

H4 is {{< var rq1.h4.decision_text >}}: Holm over {H1, H3, H4} at family-wise {{< var design.alpha.rq1_family >}} rejects H4 at its first step, at level {{< var rq1.holm.h4 >}}, with a joint HC3 Wald p {{< var rq1.h4.p_wald >}} (@tbl-rq1-confirmatory-table). The sample is {{< var rq1.h4.n >}} countries in r6 `claude_ai`. b₁ is {{< var rq1.h4.b1 >}} pp of automation per unit of log AUI (interval [{{< var rq1.h4.log_aui.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h4.log_aui.ci_high >}}], p = {{< var rq1.h4.log_aui.p >}}). b₂ is {{< var rq1.h4.b2 >}} pp of automation per unit of log GDP per working-age person (interval [{{< var rq1.h4.log_income.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h4.log_income.ci_high >}}], p = {{< var rq1.h4.log_income.p >}}). Both log coefficients are per unit of the log, not per log point. H4's direction was left open, and the negative signs are a description, not a registered prediction. Conditional on the task-mix control, countries with a higher usage index and higher income per working-age person have a lower share of classified conversations in the automation patterns. The two regressors share the working-age population in their denominators and are strongly correlated across countries. b₁ and b₂ are therefore only weakly separable one at a time, although the joint Wald test on which H4 is decided is not affected. The task-mix control's coefficient is {{< var rq1.h4.mix.estimate >}} pp per pp ([{{< var rq1.h4.mix.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h4.mix.ci_high >}}]); it is a control and is not tested. Under the pre-registered robustness row R28 for US states, the coefficients are {{< var rob.r28.us_states.log_aui.estimate >}} for log AUI (p = {{< var rob.r28.us_states.log_aui.p >}}) and {{< var rob.r28.us_states.log_income.estimate >}} for log income (p = {{< var rob.r28.us_states.log_income.p >}}). The other R28 rows are in @sec-app-robustness-tables.

The shift-share maps split each geography's gap from the global automation share into a task-mix part and a within-task part. They are descriptive, with no test attached (@fig-rq1-map-country-within; @fig-rq1-map-country-mix in @sec-app-supplementary). Across countries, the within-task part spans a wider range than the mix part. In the within-task map, Western European countries, Canada and Australia sit below the global share, and several countries in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia sit above it. Grey marks a country that is not published, and hatching marks one not published in both months; neither is ever shown as zero. @fig-rq1-map-state-mix and @fig-rq1-map-state-within (@sec-app-supplementary) draw the same split for US states. The states are not part of the H4 sample, and their regression is the R28 row above.

## The RQ1 decisions together

@tbl-rq1-confirmatory-table records the Holm sequence over {H1, H3, H4}. H4 is tested first, at {{< var rq1.holm.h4 >}}, and is supported. H1 is tested next, at {{< var rq1.holm.h1 >}}, where its null is not rejected, so the procedure stops there; H3's level is {{< var rq1.holm.h3 >}}. H2 is tested alone at {{< var rq1.holm.h2 >}} and is {{< var rq1.h2.decision_text >}}. A hypothesis that is not supported at the pre-registered level is not evidence that its coefficient is zero. The intervals above show which values the data leave open. For β_w and for H2 these include sizeable positive associations. The post-result diagnostics above (PAP §11 D-3; exploratory; not a decision) show that β_w depends on the computing occupations and that the H2 trend depends on the r2 release. How H1–H4 respond to every pre-registered robustness row is set out in @sec-robustness, and the measurement limits behind H2 are discussed in @sec-limitations.
